utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. If you'd like to take a seat. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Witness, can you please state your full name for the Court, please.

utterances.speaker: NDREC KONAJ
utterances.text: Yes. My name is Ndrec Konaj.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Mr. Konaj, where and when were you born?

utterances.speaker: NDREC KONAJ
utterances.text: I was born on December 3rd, 1954, at the Novosella e Eperme, Dukagjin.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And in which municipality and town did you live?

utterances.speaker: NDREC KONAJ
utterances.text: The municipality of Gjakove.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Can you tell us where it's located, the municipality in Kosovo, and the villages surrounding your town?

utterances.speaker: NDREC KONAJ
utterances.text: The municipality of Gjakove is about 36 kilometres from Peja, approximately 82 kilometres from Prishtina. The surrounding villages or neighbourhoods are Piskote, Brekoci, Bishtazhini.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Konaj. That's enough.

utterances.speaker: NDREC KONAJ
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And what is your profession?

utterances.speaker: NDREC KONAJ
utterances.text: I work as a building inspector.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Mr. Konaj, you were interviewed by members of the Office of the Prosecutor on 19th of April, 1999; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NDREC KONAJ
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: You were also interviewed on the 12th of June, 2001; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NDREC KONAJ
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct too.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And you gave two statements?

utterances.speaker: NDREC KONAJ
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: You attended a meeting on the 3rd of January this year in Peja, and at that meeting you were provided, by an appointed officer of the Tribunal, you were provided with a version of your statement in the Albanian language; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NDREC KONAJ
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And at that meeting, you also had an opportunity to review that statement and confirm that the contents of your two statements were true?

utterances.speaker: NDREC KONAJ
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: The Prosecution submits the two statements into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit 112, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: The summary of the witness's testimony is the following: The witness refers to incidents in 1998 when, according to the witness, Serb police damaged, looted two of his houses. On 27 March, 1999, the witness was staying at his father's house in Peja town with other relatives and friends. Around 2.00 p.m., 15 masked paramilitaries entered the yard carrying automatic weapons, grenades, and rifles with bayonets. They shot at the house, robbed the witness, and gave the occupants five minutes to leave in the direction of Montenegro. En route, the witness observed military or police at every road junction to prevent deviation from the route. The witness's group was stopped several times. On one occasion, the witness and his uncle were stopped and beaten by a group of nine men with painted faces. On another occasion, the witness was told by a Serb policeman, "There is no place for you to go other than to Montenegro." The Serbian police, army, and the paramilitary troops were located at the entrance of every street to prevent them from going back. On 28 March, 1999, the group was stopped on the outskirts of Peja by mixed Serb forces and were ordered to return to the town centre. There were thousands of people from all over Peja in the centre. About 20 trucks and buses were filled with displaced persons a number of times and set off towards Prizren. The witness got on a bus driven by an armed paramilitary. In Prizren, the displaced persons were told to leave the bus and walk to Albania. The driver said, "Go to Albania. This is not your place. This is Great Serbia." Other buses then arrived and took the displaced persons to Vermica, about 7 kilometres to the border with Albania. The witness then walked to the border, and his group was told to throw driver's licences, passports, and all other ID documents into a large box. The witness saw vehicle registration plates in the box as well. That's the summary. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It's all right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How long have you been living in Pec?

utterances.speaker: NDREC KONAJ
utterances.text: Since 1956.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Let's get it put straight. Just a moment, Mr. Milosevic. We'll see what the problem is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Where were you employed during the time that your statement encompasses, that is to say, at the beginning of 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: NDREC KONAJ
utterances.text: I was unemployed since 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, you say that the relationships between the Serbs and the Kosovars deteriorated in 1990. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NDREC KONAJ
utterances.text: Yes, they were. That is true, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Kosovo is in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: NDREC KONAJ
utterances.text: It never has been. It never will be.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Kosovo is in Serbia today too?

utterances.speaker: NDREC KONAJ
utterances.text: In your opinion it could be. In ours, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why do you say there was a deterioration in the relationships, as you say?

utterances.speaker: NDREC KONAJ
utterances.text: Because we were ill-treated for years on end. We were -- we were beaten up, attacked in every possible manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact -- do you know how many Serbs left Kosovo since, for example, 1980, up to 1990, when you say the relationships became deteriorated, under pressure and precisely because of that kind of treatment, the treatment that the Serb inhabitants had in Kosovo? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: NDREC KONAJ
utterances.text: The question is not very clear. No. Do you mean during the war?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't. What I'm asking you is whether you know that since 1980, not to go back further in time, do you know how many Serbs left Kosovo under the kind of treatment that you're talking about, but in the opposite direction, the other way around?

utterances.speaker: NDREC KONAJ
utterances.text: Did I mention ill-treatment directed towards them? Who? I'm not -- I'm not clear. Who ill-treated who?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's why I'm asking you. You mentioned the fact -- a fact that I am challenging. So I am asking you whether you know how many Serbs left before 1990, in the ten-year period from 1980 to 1990, left Kosovo because of the terror the Albanians exerted against them. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: NDREC KONAJ
utterances.text: No. This is ridiculous to allege that the Albanians have exercised any kind of terror upon the Serbian population. I'm not aware that this ever occurred. I have no knowledge of this. Even if any individual left, they left out of their own interest, probably to improve their economic situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you don't know that these Serbs left these areas, for example, the area of your municipality, the municipality of Pec, too?

utterances.speaker: NDREC KONAJ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that there are facts and figures about that, books written about it, statistics, individual cases, group cases, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He said he doesn't know, so there's no point going on about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that you lived -- in your statement, you say that you lived, after 1990 -- you said: "Our Serb neighbours used to say hello to us. We drank together, had coffee together." So when did that situation change? When did that state of affairs change for the worse? Did it happen at that time?

utterances.speaker: NDREC KONAJ
utterances.text: On the references to coffee-taking, no, no. This began in 1990, the campaign began, and the worsening of the situation vis-a-vis our neighbours. It is true that we were neighbours. They had their own land. Before 1990, it is true that we used to greet one another. But we were unaware of the intentions that came to pass, that the worst came to pass later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So when did the situation worsen, in fact?

utterances.speaker: NDREC KONAJ
utterances.text: As of 1990 onwards, and between 1998 and 1999, there was the exodus of the entire population in Kosova at large, and in Peja in particular, and this is the time when their attitude towards us worsened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that was mid-1998, as you yourself say. So from mid-1998. That's what you said. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NDREC KONAJ
utterances.text: No, not from mid-1998, but in Peja, the situation worsened to the extreme after Loxhe came under attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So Lodza was the turning point which marked the deterioration in the situation. When did that occur?

utterances.speaker: NDREC KONAJ
utterances.text: The situation had always been tense, and if you could allow me to take a document out of my own bag...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the document, Mr. Konaj, that you want to refer to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My notes, Your Honour. I've got my own notes, things that I've been unable to recall as a result of the terror and mistreatment, which makes one have difficulty remembering things. If you could permit me to consult them, given that the accused wants the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. When did you make the note?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the course of time in Kosova, after the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On July the 5th, I left my own house in the neighbourhood known as Bellopoje. And on the 6th, in the morning, Loxhe came under attack. As far as I can recall, the criminal Seselj was coming to visit Gorazhdec and one of the vehicles escorting the convoy entered Loxhe and incited the problem that resulted in the killing of a number of civilians. Whilst at 5.45 a.m. on the 6th, Loxhe came under attack by military aircraft.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And why have you called Seselj a criminal? Do you know him to be a criminal?

utterances.speaker: NDREC KONAJ
utterances.text: It is very well known that pursuant to their orders and yours, these criminal incidents occurred, these tortures occurred. Excuse me for expressing myself this way but this is the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since that is not true, because how could he order anything, let's move on. You, therefore, marked what you call the attack on Lodza as the turning point in the situation, in the state of affairs in Pec. Am I reading you correctly? It was a turning point for the worse. The situation deteriorated after that; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NDREC KONAJ
utterances.text: It had been bad all the time, but on this particular day when Loxhe came under attack, the situation became sadder with the ill-treatment and other activities that occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. As you have made a written statement, I don't see why you have to read your statement again. If you gave the statement, I assume you know what you said in it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's a matter of comment. The witness is referring to his notes to get the detail. Yes. Can we move on?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just asked for a detail and I got the detail. What he's reading now is not a detail. They are comments.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've got my own statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What did you say?

utterances.speaker: NDREC KONAJ
utterances.text: And I'm now putting it away. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You gave the statement to the investigators of the Tribunal in April 1999; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NDREC KONAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So in April 1999, you claim that the situation had worsened approximately 16 months ago, or, rather, that it took place on the first Saturday in the month of July in 1998. That's what it says. "It was the first Saturday in July 1998" is what your statement says.

utterances.speaker: NDREC KONAJ
utterances.text: Can you please clarify this? It is not very clear. Regarding the city of Peja, this -- we have -- the suggestion has always been worse. But I mentioned earlier, on the 5th of July, when Loxhe came under attack, at that point the entire city became three times more -- three times more worse, as it were, because of the siege of Serbian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So according to you, the situation was three times worse because the attack on Lodza, according to what you say. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: NDREC KONAJ
utterances.text: They came, but as many as three times more reinforcements of Serbian forces. The ill-treatment, beatings, enigmatic killings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I have heard about those expressions that the other witnesses used too, but what I'm interested in is the facts. Now, do you know - I'm sure you must know as a citizen of Pec - that the attack on Lodza was organised by the leadership of the KLA and that that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Let the witness answer. Do you know that this attack was organised by the leadership of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that's not at all true. It's known very well that police vehicles, as I said before, they escorted Seselj's convoy. And one of these vehicles entered the road at the junction from Gorazhdec that goes to Loxhe, and there they met some young kids who were playing with a ball in the road, and they were witnesses of what happened. And then they maltreated these kids. And Tahir Shalaj was killed on that same day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know the name of Tahir Zemaj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. Your Honour, excuse me. Shall I explain more clearly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What's the question, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Do you know the name of Tahir Zemaj?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What's the significance of this name?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The significance of this name is that Tahir Zemaj was the chief commander of the units that carried out the attack on Lodza. His deputy was the notorious bandit Ramush Haradinaj and--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness has said that it was not -- it did not take place in the way that you suggested. So there's no point going on putting things to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that in your sources, the KLA calls the Lodza battle, as they refer to it, as one of the most professional operations carried out by the KLA? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: NDREC KONAJ
utterances.text: No, I don't know this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that the 134th Brigade took part in that battle, precisely according to the information provided by the KLA command? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: NDREC KONAJ
utterances.text: No, I don't know about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is not part of his statement. It comes in as a result of your cross-examination. We should return to the statement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, haven't we all heard here that the battle in Lodza was the turning point for the worse, and this is one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have heard that. It comes in as a result of your cross-examination and you have examined the witness about it. You've put your case to him. It seems to be a waste of the Court's time to go on further. He wasn't there. He's merely telling what he heard. And I suggest we move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since you heard that a battle had taken place, between who did this battle take place in Lodza?

utterances.speaker: NDREC KONAJ
utterances.text: The Serbian police and army against innocent civilians in the village of Loxhe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that your own commanders, who are now publicly writing about that battle, speak of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to stop this. The witness is merely accounting what he heard. It doesn't assist the Trial Chamber. If it's relevant, you can call evidence about it in due course, but this has gone on for more than 20 minutes. You've only got one hour. You should be concentrating on what's in the statement from now on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, please bear in mind - and I wish to highlight that - since he said that this was a key issue, a turning point, in terms of the deterioration of the situation, and since this is the most flagrant possible twisting of facts, and there is irrefutable evidence about this, including books published by KLA commanders --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is all argument. The witness has given his evidence. This is what he said is true and what happened. You've had the opportunity to cross-examine him about it. Now it's time to move on to another issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know the name of Ramabaja?

utterances.speaker: NDREC KONAJ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know the name of Stojkaj?

utterances.speaker: NDREC KONAJ
utterances.text: I know that they're from Decan municipality somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know the name of Hadri Djonaj?

utterances.speaker: NDREC KONAJ
utterances.text: I come from Peja municipality, not from Decan municipality, and I know my own area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about Pec; not about who was born in Pec, but who did something in Pec. Do you know the name of Farush Thaci?

utterances.speaker: NDREC KONAJ
utterances.text: This question is not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you whether you know the name of that man. Do you know that man, Farush Thaci?

utterances.speaker: NDREC KONAJ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know the name of a man called Salih Ceku?

utterances.speaker: NDREC KONAJ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know the name of Rrustem Buci?

utterances.speaker: NDREC KONAJ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And have you heard of Shaban Shala?

utterances.speaker: NDREC KONAJ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What about Hasan Kamaja? Have you heard of him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's enough of these lists. He doesn't know these people.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are names of commanders of units of the KLA who at that time, precisely at the time about which this witness has been saying the most incredible things, were attacking Lodza, with major forces, with the intention of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I've told you to move on. Now, unless you've got some different questions for this witness, we'll conclude the examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have many other different questions. Don't worry about that. I just have one question, because the witness was a building inspector, he finished school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that a book came out published by Mergimi in the year 2000 - this is a mere photocopy, though - and the book is called "Thus Spoke Tahir Zemaj: Comments About the War."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the other names.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of this book that you published in 2000?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Are you suggesting -- just one moment. Are you suggesting the witness published it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, I'm not saying that. The same people who sent him here published the book in order to portray events in this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is a comment. Do you know anything about this book?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that it's been published, but I've never actually seen a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that in that book is information given by your commanders? And recoilless guns are mentioned there, heavy guns, heavy armaments, all these other things --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He doesn't know anything about it, and it's quite wrong to refer to "your commanders," quite wrong. There's no evidence of that. Now, you could put the book in front of us, for what it's worth, in due course, if you wish to. Meanwhile, we should continue with this examination on a different topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I highlight this, I mention recoilless guns and heavy weapons that they mention here, precisely because the witness said, only a short while ago, that the army and police clashed with unarmed civilians, and it was numerous units of the KLA that took part in that, and they attacked Lodza. And in that book --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to stop this examination unless you move to another topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if it is quite clear that the witness is saying a total untruth --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... it's for us to decide. Now, move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. It would be the same thing as if you were to decide on whether today is Saturday or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When did you send your older son to Switzerland?

utterances.speaker: NDREC KONAJ
utterances.text: Before July, sometime towards the beginning of February, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As for the month of July, you marked it as the point when things turned for the worse, and you said that in April, the next year, the following year, after less than ten months, or rather, eight months, you stated that the situation abruptly turned for the worse 16 months prior to that. How is that possible? Is that your statement from April or some later statement?

utterances.speaker: NDREC KONAJ
utterances.text: Your Honour, the accused is confusing things up. I was very plain in what I said. I said that the attack on Loxhe took place on the 5th of July. On the 6th, there were attacks from the air by helicopter. I sent my son to Switzerland earlier --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have your evidence on that point. Yes, Mr. Milosevic. What's the next question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who is the person called Lorenz Konaj?

utterances.speaker: NDREC KONAJ
utterances.text: It's my brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Where does he live?

utterances.speaker: NDREC KONAJ
utterances.text: Are you really interested? Shall I tell him, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, unless there's any relevance in this. Where did he live in 1998 or 1999? Can you help us with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course. He was in Germany. He was harried there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What did he do in relation to the KLA?

utterances.speaker: NDREC KONAJ
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know of any activity of his related to the organisation of the KLA and related to his life in Germany?

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Unless there is any relevance of the family of the accused, I think it --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, might we raise a point on this? If it's a matter of influence over this particular witness, then it may be a legitimate route of questioning for the accused to go down. That's what we would say on his behalf.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll allow these questions providing the relevance Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. can be established. Yes, Mr. Milosevic. You must ask some questions to establish any relevance of this and then you can put directly what you say about the brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So my direct question is: Does he know about the participation of his brother in the organisation of the KLA related to his stay in Germany?

utterances.speaker: NDREC KONAJ
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said in your statement, in relation to this first Saturday in the month, that your wife had a premonition that something bad would happen, and it was according to this premonition of his -- of hers that you sent your mother and two daughters to your father's house, which is in Pec. And after that, you and your wife left your house and also went to your father's house. All of that happened during the same day, if I read it correctly.

utterances.speaker: NDREC KONAJ
utterances.text: That's not quite right. The truth is as follows: My -- I sent away my wife [as interpreted] and two daughters two months ago to the Karagac neighbourhood, whereas my wife and I stayed where we were in the neighbourhood Bellopoje, until the 5th of July when, because this -- because this area had been surrounded and -- and everybody stayed around the cemeteries. On the very same day, on the 5th of July, my wife would not agree to spend the night there and so I insisted that we join the mother and our daughters. On the very next day, we heard of the attack at Loxhe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this coincides with the information provided here. You left your house just before the attack, practically a few hours before the attack. If you left the previous day and if the attack took place in the early morning, one could say that this was only a few hours prior to the attack; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NDREC KONAJ
utterances.text: Yes, before, but we were unaware that Loxhe would come under attack. There was no fighting whatsoever. It was -- it was at the insistence of my wife that we left. And we went through the cemeteries of Muslims and the Catholics on the lower part of the cemeteries, which were full of armed civilians and paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you had not been informed that an attack would take place on Lodza. You left prior to the attack because of the premonition of your wife. That is what you've been claiming.

utterances.speaker: NDREC KONAJ
utterances.text: I was not aware. Let me reiterate. I had no contacts or conversations, because we were staying indoors, in the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you did not have any contacts, any talks with anyone from the KLA?

utterances.speaker: NDREC KONAJ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Saqir Studenica, did he tell you who had looted your house and damaged it?

utterances.speaker: NDREC KONAJ
utterances.text: Saqir Studenica told me that my house had been attacked and that he had sent the corpse of the late Naxhije Hoti there. She's the mother of my neighbour, killed by the police at the Petran object, one of those where vehicles were checked. This happened on the Tuesday, not on July the 5th. She was killed on Monday, and on Tuesday Saqir Studenica told me about it, because police came to the house of my uncle's, looking for my son, and then I went myself there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And why did the police come to your uncle's place to look for his sons if they were living at your address?

utterances.speaker: NDREC KONAJ
utterances.text: That woman who was killed and sent into the balcony of my house, it was alleged that my -- "Your son has killed a policeman." My uncle emerged to say that is not true, because he has not been here for a long while. And so they forced my uncle to go and identify the victim.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How come your son was suspected of having killed that woman and he was not anywhere nearby?

utterances.speaker: NDREC KONAJ
utterances.text: The accused should ask the police about that, because that's what they said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I understand this, the police was acting upon the instructions of the investigating judge in the course of the investigation of the killing of this woman, and your son was a suspect. Are you aware of that or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You needn't answer that. Mr. Milosevic, you've spent three-quarters of an hour dealing with events in July 1998 which are of peripheral relevance to this witness's evidence. If you wish to challenge his account, his substantial account of events in March 1999, you should do so in the quarter of an hour remaining to you for examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I think that there is no need for me to repeat that I absolutely contest everything that this witness has said, just like other witnesses who are not telling the truth. From the very beginning of these hearings here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No need to make a speech about it, but if you want to ask him about what happened in March, you should do so now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The second thing I wish to have clarified is the following: I assume that it is not forbidden to have me question one witness for a shorter period of time and another witness for a longer period of time but if it all adds up to the amount of time allocated to me. I hope that this is something that you won't mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It is something we will take into account, but the normal rule would be a one-hour maximum.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You planned one hour, if that's the maximum, and then you planned for four 92 bis witnesses to be heard today; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There is no plan as to how many witnesses there should be. But let us move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I was thinking that within this time that you have allocated to me, I should economise in a more rational way, but all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did your sons have a criminal record on the territory of the SFRY, the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's not a relevant question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Never. Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, then, why did the police take your uncle Anton Konaj on that day to your house?

utterances.speaker: NDREC KONAJ
utterances.text: They asked the uncle to go and identify the corpse that they had placed in the balcony of my own house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since you had heard that your house had been damaged and looted, why did you go to your uncle's first and then only to the police station so that you would say what was going on, as you had put it?

utterances.speaker: NDREC KONAJ
utterances.text: Not on what had happened, because the police had come into the house at daylight and done what they did. This is not true. I went to my own house to inquire about what the police were about, because the police were unable to get in contact with me. They got in contact with Shaqir Studenica who came to me, and both of us went to the house. Upon arrival, my uncle told me that if I did not go to the police, they were bound to come again at any time; at night, in the morning. And so I decided to go and report at the police station. My uncle came with me. Upon arriving there, one of the policemen said there was no need, because we are aware who did this, and you should not go to your own properties. And at that moment the uncle came, asked, "How about our own houses?" And at that moment, the policeman insulted him, and then I took my uncle and both of us left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how did the policeman attack him?

utterances.speaker: NDREC KONAJ
utterances.text: He insulted him, basically, on his mother's name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So he cursed him, he swore at him?

utterances.speaker: NDREC KONAJ
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. He said, "'F' your Albanian mother," and then at that moment I just took my own uncle and went out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when did you leave Kosovo to go to Montenegro, actually?

utterances.speaker: NDREC KONAJ
utterances.text: In 1998, I left Kosova twice. That is to say, on the 9th or the 10th, on a Friday, in the morning, before leaving as a result of police patrols coming to inquire about us at my father's, before departing for Montenegro, my wife and me went to the graveyard, where a neighbour said, "Do not go to your own houses." And at that moment my wife, with the neighbour's wife, went to a different house, where a Macedonian married to a Serb lived, and she escorted them to my own house just to be able to see whether the corpse was still in the balcony. Upon arriving there, they emerged from the windows, asked, "Where are you heading to?" And she said, "To my own house." And then she went in and saw everything that had been demolished, walls full of graffiti: "Welcome back," "Serbia reaches up to Tirana," and so on and so forth. At that point, we departed for Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you say that before you left, your house was taken over by snipers?

utterances.speaker: NDREC KONAJ
utterances.text: Yes, it is true. The other two were demolished and destroyed, and the Court has got photographs of it. They were one-storey buildings, whilst the unfinished, new houses were the locations where the snipers were positioned, not only these two houses but another three or four in that very same neighbourhood, and they had an overview over the whole territory of Loxhe and Peja.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who were those people in your house, the snipers who took over your house? Who were they?

utterances.speaker: NDREC KONAJ
utterances.text: We were not in a position to go and see who they were, because had we encountered them, we don't know what the end result would have been. They were called Frenki.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did you say a moment ago that your wife just found graffiti written up on the walls of your house? You were talking about your own house, or did I misunderstand you?

utterances.speaker: NDREC KONAJ
utterances.text: The graffiti on the walls and the doors of the house were in Serbo-Croatian. It is very clear from the photographs. The Serbian police and the army, whoever was there, had written them. I wasn't there to verify who, which one of the parties did that, but it was very clear what was written: "From here to Tirana, it's Serbia," "This is Serbia," "We'll be back."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: "We'll be back." Well, what does that mean, "We'll be back"? It means that somebody had written that who had left the place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Not for the witness to speculate as to what the meaning of graffiti is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the occasion, did you see a lot of houses that were burnt, damaged, from the effects of -- in that part of Lodza?

utterances.speaker: NDREC KONAJ
utterances.text: On the 6th of July, we were only able to see things from a distance, from afar, from my father's. We were only to see smoke, and smoke specks were reaching up the city, because the place had come under attack by military aircraft. And I don't know why you ask this question, because a number of houses must have been burnt. Loxhe was completely flattened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You used the same expression that was used by these commanders, KLA commanders here, because they said that they ordered everything to be flattened to the ground and set fire to, in this book here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's a matter of comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking him whether there is any link and relevance, that is to say, that you're using the same expression that they used in the book, "flattened."

utterances.speaker: NDREC KONAJ
utterances.text: Helicopters and military aircraft with Serbian insignia. Who else? Who else could have procured that, apart from your own army and the police who bombed them that day, who bombed the entire village?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And those commanders of yours write and say that their fighters in the battle with the Serb forces did that. That's what they say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You have insisted on continuing a line of cross-examination which you were told was of little relevance, and as a result, I'm bringing this cross-examination to an end. You're continually reverting to the same point in your case. Now, have the amici any questions? No, no more questions. No. Have the amici any questions?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I have 50 more questions for this man.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Any re-examination? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. It's just one matter. If the Court needs the photos that the witness is referring to -- the Prosecution didn't want to submit the photos because they are outside of the period of the indictment, but for clarification of the graffiti, if the Court needs, we'll have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And thank you for bringing them, Mr. Konaj, but we've heard the evidence, and it is more than sufficient. Thank you for coming. You're free to go now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we bring the other witness, I just would like to clarify one matter. I wanted to let the Court know that one of the witnesses, the third one, Mahmut Halimi, he had to be taken to the hospital for an exam. So right now, during the morning, he is in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Sorry. I've just been informed that he arrived from the hospital, so we won't have to change the order of the witness. Sorry about that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Who is the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: It's Edison Zatriqi.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecutor kindly provide a resume to the interpreters, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Yes, I will take care of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Witness, can you please state your full name to the Court.

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: My name is Edison Zatriqi.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Where and when were you born?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: I was born on 5th of December, 1956, in Peja.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: In which municipality is Peja located?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: Peja is a municipality in itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And can you describe the villages surrounding Peja?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: There are a lot of villages in Peja municipality. There is Loxhe, Rahociq, and then Cisk [phoen], Pavlani, Radafc.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Thank you. What is your profession?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: At the moment, I am a driver for the regional office of the OSCE in Peja.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And you are an Albanian?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Mr. Zatriqi, you were interviewed by members of the Office of the Prosecutor on the 20th of June, 2001; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Did you give a statement at that time?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: On the 29th of January this year, you attended a meeting in Peja before members of the Office of the Prosecutor and an appointed officer of the Tribunal, and at that meeting you were provided with an Albanian copy of your statement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: You reviewed your statement, and you also made an addendum to correct minor mistakes from your first statement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I corrected the errors at that time, and they were translation mistakes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: The summary of the witness's testimony is the following: The witness is a lifelong resident of Peja and was a director of a coach company named Flamingo Tours, which owned three coaches. On 23 March 1999, the witness was ordered to the company yard by Serb police who took away the three coaches. When the witness asked for documentary confirmation, one of the policemen pointed his gun at the witness and threatened him. He did not see the vehicles again until he returned to Peja after the armed conflict. The witness subsequently found out that his buses had been used to transport Kosovo Albanians out of Peja. The witness also describes that on 27 March 1999, he was in his house when he saw Serb military firing shells from the hospital yard and secondary school towards the area of Kapeshnica. The witness moved to the home of a relative in another neighbourhood. The following day, 28th of March, the witness and his family drove to Rozaje, Montenegro, in a long convoy of vehicles. En route, they passed armed police and civilians who were directing them. The witness left Kosovo as he feared for his safety and that of his family. He returned to Peja on 26 July 1999 to find his home, business offices, and coaches completely burnt out. This is the summary. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. The statement should be exhibited.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry, Your Honour. We submit the statements.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is Exhibit 113, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the accused, please. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused speak into the microphone, please. We did not hear the beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you start again? The interpreters didn't hear the beginning.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the accused please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you spent your whole life in Pec and that you dealt in the field of transport; that is to say, you communicated a great deal in that environment. You went to and fro. Can we assume that you are well acquainted with the situation in Pec and that you were well acquainted with the situation in Pec prior to the war?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: It's true that I've spent all my life in Peja, but I haven't always been involved in transport. I became involved in transport after I was dismissed from the Ljubljana bank from where I was dispensed in 1991, and then I started as a driver. It is true that I travelled a lot, around a large part of the Balkans apart -- as far as Austria, Italy, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The point of my question was to say that you were well acquainted with the situation and circumstances in Pec and as they were just before the war; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: Yes. Relatively well. I'm relatively well-informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And the fact that before working in transport you worked in the Slovenia bank was also a job which meant communicating with people and learning quite a bit in the process; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What were, during those pre-war years, the relationships in Pec like? Can you tell us briefly in one or two sentences? Describe what the relationships were like.

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: I can answer, but you must make clear in which period of time, whether it's before you came to power or afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the period just before the war. Now, you can talk about whatever period you like, but what I'm asking you is just before the war, the period just prior to the war, which means 1998, 1999, to be more specific.

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: Even though this period was a very difficult one because our movements were very restricted at this time, relations between the Albanians and the Serbs were very chilly. They were especially chilly after the mysterious murders that started in Peja in 1998 with the murder of the Gjuka brothers, the murder of Dr. Ceku, the murder of Dr. Xhevad Gashi, and of Emin Basha. This led to relations cooling considerably.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who killed these Albanians, the Albanians that you've just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: In this period, particularly in Peja, this was an open secret. These murders were directed and carried out by a notorious organisation called the Black Hand, which, particularly at dusk and at dawn, it kidnapped Albanians that were on the streets accidently and then nothing more was heard of them. And they may well -- they were often found the next day, dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know which Black Hand organisation you're talking about. We know about one organisation called Crna Ruka, or Black Hand, which dates back a hundred years. And that one ceased to exist a long time ago. It has joined the rank of history. So what Black Hand are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: I don't know anything about the Black Hand organisation which was formed 120 years ago, but I know that it continued its work in Peja, and its members were regular policemen who during the day did police work and during the night committed cruel murders in our city.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what is it that you're looking for in the papers you have in front of you? Are you looking for the Black Hand, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: No. Fortunately, I did not experience the work of the Black Hand in Peja before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, do tell us, then, please. Do tell us, then, please, at least who told you about this Black Hand.

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: There was a lot of talk about the Black Hand in Peja at that time, and I can say I've got a few members of this organisation here in my notes, and they included my neighbours. And as I said before, there was a lot of talk about this organisation in our city.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just help with us this, Mr. Zatriqi: What are the notes which you have in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These notes that I have are about the period before the war and the moment of my deportation along with my fellow citizens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And when did you make the notes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I made these notes at the time when these events happened. All the notes I had, I put into a computer and then printed them out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, might I assist the Court that the notes there look handwritten to me, and on the top of the page. We seem to be having a succession of witnesses now bringing notes into the courtroom, and one really questions whether that is desirable, given the fact that this is cross-examination by the accused at this stage, the witnesses have their statement produced as exhibits, a summary given to the Court, and it might be more helpful to the proceedings if they just answered the questions unaided rather than referring to notes that may well have a different history and background that could cloud the issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, this would meet your requirement of contemporaneity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We haven't really gone into this in great detail with the witness, as to when, and scrutinised the document and questioned him upon it as to when it actually arose and whether matters were fresh in his mind at the time. I take Your Honour's point that it well may be an issue of contemporaneity here. Notes, of course, can have a long period of time to justify contemporaneity. It's the issue, really, with which I raise the matter to the Court, because it may be unhelpful to the evidence if such material is going to be relied upon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I mention that, Mr. Kay, because even when the notes do not meet that requirement, with which you're familiar in your system, we sometimes allow witnesses to refresh their memories from notes which are made even subsequent to the event, because ultimately we have to assess the weight that is to be given to the evidence. But I think we'll consult on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Zatriqi, we will allow you to refer to your notes, but if you can, give your evidence without reference to them, because it's Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. your evidence we want, not what's written in your notes. But if you need to refresh your memory on a particular point, you can do so. And Ms. Romano, as far as the witnesses are concerned, perhaps the better course would be, in future, that if they want to refer to their notes particularly, then they can ask permission to do so, if they've made notes and brought them along. But on the whole, the witnesses, of course, should give evidence without notes, but simply giving it. So if the Prosecution would take note of that, and in future, if they want to, they perhaps should mention it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just want to clarify that when they come to The Hague, they come with several material accompanied, and the instruction of the Prosecution is in the same lines, that what is important is their evidence. But sometimes, you know, they just come to the Court because they feel afraid of forgetting. It's more of a helpful tool.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, if they want --

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: I will take care.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If they want to provide it - if they were made roughly at the time - if they want to refer to it, they can, but they should ask.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: We'll take care of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll adjourn now. It's past the time. Mr. Zatriqi, we're going to adjourn for half an hour. During the adjournment, please remember not to speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over, and that does include members of the Prosecution team. We'll adjourn for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. THE ACCUSED [Interpretation] Since you took a break after you conferred about the notes, I would just wish to state that nowhere in the witness's statement, the two written statements he gave, has it been said that he used notes while giving his statement. If he didn't do it then, I don't understand why he would do it now. That goes for other witnesses as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you want to ask him about it, you can.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am stating that in the statement, there is no mention of that, because I assume that if the witness had resorted to notes while giving his statement, it would have to be noted by your official. All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. So you spoke of the atmosphere, the atmosphere that was hampered by crimes. You mentioned some unresolved killings, murders. My question is: Do you know that these killings were committed by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: No. You are wrong. These were not committed by the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How come you know that it wasn't the KLA that did it when you say, no, that it wasn't the KLA? That means that you know that they didn't do it.

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: First, don't interrupt me but listen to me. Listen to my answers to the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, listen, Mr. Zatriqi. You must remember you're in a court. And just answer the questions, if you please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My answer is as I said before, that it was an open secret in Peja, and we knew that this organisation was working in Peja in 1998 and 1999. And at this time, we didn't even dare to go out of our houses. Or when we went out, we did so for very short periods.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that this rumour about the alleged Black Hand was precisely launched by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We are really getting a very long way from this case, particularly talking about rumour and the like. Now, can we move on to something which is more relevant?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I refer to rumours because the witness spoke about them. Now let us go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You knew people who were in top positions in Pec. Were there many Albanians in top positions in Pec?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: From the time when you came into power, you could number them on the fingers of your hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I'm asking you, from that period onwards and not only from that period onwards, I'm asking you about 1998 and 1999, do you know Albanians in Pec who were in top positions, who held various offices in government in Pec? Just say yes or no in order to save time.

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: In this period 1998, 1999, I don't know of anybody who had a significant position in Peja.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Have you heard of the name of Xhafer Gjuka?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: Yes. He was my physical education teacher at grammar school in Peja.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was he head of social services in the municipality of Pec and also, later on, a member of the provisional council of Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: I didn't know about Xhafer Gjuka's position, but I know that he was involved in a party called JUL or something like that, but I don't know what his position was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He was a member of the leadership of the Yugoslav left, but he held these positions. So you do not know that he was a member of the provisional council and also that he was head of social services in Pec?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know of another Albanian, Deme Muhaj, who was deputy head of state security in Pec? Do you know him?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: I knew him as a person, but you've got his surname wrong. It's not Muhaj, but Mujaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not quite certain, when I read an Albanian name, whether I've pronounced it accurately, but it's important that we have identified him. Do you know of Shaqir Nikqi, Shaqir Nikqi, who was a misdemeanours judge in Pec?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: No, I didn't know him. This is the first time I've heard his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know Mazllum Avdyli? Who is Mazllum Avdyli?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: I don't remember him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Principal of the school in Pec. And do you know who is Rizah Demaj, principal of the primary school?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: Tell me which primary school, because I don't remember this name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The primary school in Rogovo, near Pec.

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: No, I don't remember him. I don't know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since you were involved in business, you probably know the name of Fatmir Gashi. He was deputy director of the SDK, the public accounting service in Pec.

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: Yes, I know Fatmir Gashi personally. He was a colleague of mine when we worked in the bank. And there was not only Fatmir, but there were many others in the social accounting service.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Also Albanians; right?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: I don't understand this comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. What is the relevance of all this? What this witness said in his evidence, and the significance of it, is that he was director of a coach company, the coaches of which were taken from him and used, the Prosecution say, to deport refugees; and that he was himself, in March of 1999, when he was in Pec, he was there when there was shelling, and he left in his family car and went to Montenegro. Now, that's what his evidence is about. You're trying to extend it to matters which seem to me, speaking for myself, to be totally irrelevant. What's the relevance of the fact that, even if so, that there may have been some Albanians in some positions in Pec at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the relevance is in the fact that the witness has been claiming that Albanians were in high positions earlier on and that later on their number was a single-digit one. And then also he said just before the war, in 1998, 1999, there weren't any in high positions that he knew of. I have here a list of a great many Albanians who held very significant positions in Pec. He was a director of a company. Pec is not New York City, so he would have to know all these Albanians. The question has to do with the credibility of his statement. When the witness says that there weren't any Albanians in high positions and when he is shown these facts, he would have to admit that, because it was not a single-digit number, it was a double-digit number, and even more than that, including one Albanian, as you heard, who was a member of the government. That's very important here, because the impression is being created that the Albanians had no rights whatsoever. And we see here that in a big town, Pec, a large number of Albanians held very important positions, public offices, administrative jobs, et cetera. That is why it is relevant. If you claim that all of this is irrelevant, well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Even if you were right about that, this Court is concerned with displacement and killings in 1999. Now, some evidence of events before then may of course be relevant, but these seem to me matters of not a great deal of significance, and a lot of the Court's time is being taken up with them, the case of the last witness and now here again with this one. If you've got something to challenge about what the witness said happened in his statement, then you should put it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the relevance of these questions is also in the fact that these facts fully bring under a question mark the stories about deportations, because these persons in high positions -- I mean, had there been any deportations, these persons in high offices would have had to be engaged, involved in these deportations because they held such important positions. And who would believe that, that Albanians who are part of government in a municipality would organise deportations of Albanians, even if it were to be assumed that the Serbs wanted to do that, which is also not true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you challenge the way in which this witness has given an account of leaving for Macedonia? If so, you should put it. And do you challenge that his vehicles were sequestrated? Do you challenge that? If so, you should put it to him. That's the matters with which he can deal and those are the matters which are relevant.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, isn't it clear that I'm challenging it? And I hope that if you carefully read both of his witness statements, you will also be perfectly clear that his very statements challenge that. But we'll show that. Please just tell me how far time you're giving me for this witness so that I could cut my questions short, because obviously I will not be in a position to put all the questions I have for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You have the usual time for the witness, and so far you've taken up, I should think, 20 minutes of it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. So I have another 40 minutes for him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Something of that order, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. That is to say, until 12.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then I shall briefly scan all of this, and then you're going to tell me whether you know any of these people. Do you know the names of Skender Nuro, director of the company called Zitopromet; Besim Haska, deputy head of the sales inspection in the district; Muhammed Corkadiu, who was president of the municipality of Pec and then head of the planning and analysis department in Pec; Skender Hajdini, head of the personnel department in Pec, that is to say, the person who admitted officials for work and released them; Dr. Drita, who was head of a ward; Fatmir Kurmehaj, also a director of the hospital --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Stop. Mr. Zatriqi, what is being suggested is that there were Albanians who were in important positions in Pec. Now, can you help us about that or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. All the names mentioned by the accused are people known to me, but I must say these positions cannot be compared with the position of Fatmir Gashi, who is an able economist. There was no way of comparing this with the position of Xhafer Gjuka, because these are absolute opposites. And I don't know much about the inner workings of the municipality because I didn't have much dealings with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand the explanation of these opposites. Xhafer Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Gjuka, isn't he an Albanian too?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: Xhafer Gjuka is an Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He was a member of the provisional government of Kosovo. So why would this be in opposition to the other Albanian who was director of the SDK?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of Xhafer Gjuka's position, but I didn't know he had such a high position. I knew him as a deputy director in the public accounting service.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, then, all these Albanians whose names I've read out to you, did you know all of them?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: Not all of them. Some of them I did know but as citizens of Peja, as faces. Some of them I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that you didn't know what they did? You don't know what positions they held? Is that your assertion?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: No, I didn't know what jobs they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I don't want to waste much time. I'm just going to read ten more names of Albanians to you so that you tell me whether you know them. Dr. Midhat Jakupi, head of the orthopaedics department of the city hospital; Ojdaj [phoen] Pepa, the secretary of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker please slow down for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Adem Grapci, municipal -- Judge of the municipal court in Pec; Shaban Ukaj, coordinator for education in Pec. Claims were always made that Albanians were not being educated, but even the head of education in Pec was an Albanian. Sali Dionka, director of the cooperative in Kucica. Not to mention all of them. There are five directors of cooperatives in villages around Pec, and all of them are Albanians. At the head of the military department in Pec was also an Albanian. That is to say, the lists of military conscripts, call-up papers were sent by Hatixhe Berisha, Ekrem Zara, inspector --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Enough. The witness cannot begin to take all this in.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am asking him --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Zatriqi, you've been asked about a list of names. Can you help about those or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Some of them I know, but I can't know who was in what position. For instance, manager of a cooperative. I was involved in transport and had nothing to do with agriculture. And he could read out a lot of other names, but I wouldn't know what positions they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you know of Hatixhe Berisha at least, the military department in Pec? That is to say, military conscripts, their lists, call-up polices for the army, et cetera. He was an ethnic Albanian. Do you know of that?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: No. I don't know anything about him. I completed my military service a long time ago, and I don't know anything about All People's Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You were involved in transportation. Do you know the name of Fetih Hoti and Ekrem Zara? Both of them worked precisely as inspectors for transportation in the municipality of Pec. That is to say, your own line of work. Also Albanians.

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: Yes, I know him personally. And I know that his authorities were very restricted. He had been inspector for years. And there was another inspector called Antic. And Fetih Hoti had very limited responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. As far as responsibilities are concerned, that's a very relative question. I can't really read all this out to you because it would be pointless, but so far I have read out at least 30 names to you or, rather, positions that were held by Albanians. Doesn't it seem to you that with that structure of positions that were held by Albanians, some government can be involved in the organisation of deportations of Albanians from Pec?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's not a matter for the witness. It's a matter that we'll have to decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that in the villages around Pec there were local policemen, precisely in Albanian villages, that were elected by the citizens themselves, the local villagers, and who held these positions of local policemen who wore uniforms and who carried weapons? They were selected by the villagers in those respective villages? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: No. I do not remember this, because in Peja and its environs, I have never come across an Albanian policeman, and I've had contacts with loads of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember the name of Haxha Berisha from the village of Krusevac?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: No, I cannot remember this name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He was a local policeman, an Albanian in the village of Krusevac. And what about Gaci Kelmendi? Have you heard of that name?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: No. I have not heard of any name of anybody who, as you allege, was a policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He was in the village of Kosoric. What about the name of Bushataj? Bushataj, a local policeman for the Llubeniq and Rausic villages which are right by Pec? He was killed by members of the KLA precisely because he was a policeman. Do you know of that event?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: No. I haven't heard of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What about a policeman named Nikoliqi for the Dragovan, Milovanic, and Pocesje villages? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: No. I have not known him. And as you very well know, I lived in Peja, and during 1998, 1999, I did not go through these villages in particular. These names are not known to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As you were just in Pec, do you know of a single Serb civilian, a policeman or soldier during this period of time, let's say October 1998 and the 24th of March, 1999, was killed or abducted by the KLA from the Pec area?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: No, I haven't heard. I haven't heard of that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Have you heard of the KLA at all? Did you hear of it while you were in Pec at all?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: Yes, a lot, and I am proud of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You've given your answer. Now, do you know about the killing -- the killing of children in the Panda Bar in Pec? A boy was killed. He was -- boys were killed, the ages of 17 to 19.

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: Yes, I've heard of this incident. And this is one of the questionable murders that occurred in my city.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you know anything yourself about it directly or is it merely things that you've heard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are things that were spoken about around Peja and which I've heard of. Can I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What's the next question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Have you heard of Sadriu Komoni?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: No. I don't know him, and I can't remember this name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know what his relations were with the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: In my answer, I said that I did not know this person, hence there's no way of knowing what kind of relations he had with the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know of an Albanian by the name of Thaci Uka?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: No. Haven't heard -- haven't heard of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know of an Albanian by the name of Bushati Jahu?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI
utterances.text: No. I haven't known him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And have you at least heard that Bushati Jahu, as a member of the KLA, killed Thaci Uka? That is something that you must have heard about in Pec.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He says he doesn't know him. He doesn't know about these kind of matters. Can we move on to something more relevant?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, everybody in Pec knows what the other person is having for lunch, is cooking for lunch, let alone when somebody kills somebody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is that true of Pec, or Peja?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
